Onboarding for CPDSE-teachers

Where, What, How

CPDSE uses three reference models to plan its course upgrades and its People Development workshops (training for staff already in post). This page explains why there are three, how they fit together, and where to look things up.

Before you start · Connections

Start from your own teaching

Before looking at any model, think of one course or workshop you teach, or would like to teach. Keep it in mind as you read.

  1. Where

    Which part of drug development does it prepare people for?

  2. What

    What should people be able to do afterwards, and how well?

  3. How

    How will they practise it, rather than only hear about it?

Those three questions are the three models. The rest of this page shows how they fit together.

This page is itself planned with the teaching model it describes. The small labels above each part (Connections, Concepts, Concrete Practice, Conclusions) are Sharon Bowman's 4Cs, explained under How.

Next: One sentence, three models ↓

Part 1 of 4 · Concepts · about 2 min

One sentence, three models

To improve capabilities in the pharma value chain, we train and catalyse data-science competencies using Training from the Back of the Room practices.

This sentence is how CPDSE describes its method. Each marked phrase is one reference model, and each model answers one of your three questions. (PDS stands for Pharmaceutical Data Science. Training from the Back of the Room is a teaching approach by Sharon Bowman in which participants, not the teacher, do most of the work.)

  • Where

    Pharma Value Chain

    Where in drug development?

    Anchors a course or workshop to the substeps it prepares people for.

    3 steps, 14 substeps · v0.8.0, draft

  • What

    PDS Competence Model

    What should people be able to do?

    Describes Pharmaceutical Data Science (PDS) capabilities, so we can assess today's level and set a target.

    7 domains, 30 sub-areas, 123 competencies · levels L1–L5

  • How

    Pedagogic Practices

    How do we build it so it sticks?

    Shapes every session so participants do the work themselves, because the person doing the work does the learning.

    Bowman's 4Cs (a four-part session plan) and Six Trumps (six rules of thumb) · v0.1.1, draft

Why three models, not one

Every course or workshop has to answer where, what and how. One model that tried to cover all three would become vague, so each question has its own model. Each model is also self-contained, so it can change without breaking the others.

For every course or workshop we help design, we combine them in the same order: anchor it in the value chain, assess current levels and set targets, then deliver the teaching. That shared order keeps CPDSE's work consistent across teachers, courses and partners. Curriculum courses and People Development workshops use the same three models; only the balance between them differs.

Key idea: one model per question, combined in the same order every time.

Next: Take one away ↓

Part 2 of 4 · Concepts · about 1 min

Take one away

The quickest way to see why all three models matter is to take one away at a time.

  1. Without Where

    • Where (missing)
    • What
    • How

    Good teaching, wrong context

    A general machine-learning module that pharmacy students can't connect to drug discovery.

  2. Without What

    • Where
    • What (missing)
    • How

    Engaging, but aimless

    A lively staff workshop with no starting level and no target, so nobody can say what improved.

  3. Without How

    • Where
    • What
    • How (missing)

    Right content, doesn't stick

    A well-targeted course taught as lectures and forgotten by the exam.

  4. All three models

    • Where
    • What
    • How

    Relevant, measurable, lasting

    A CPDSE course upgrade or People Development workshop.

Key idea: without Where the teaching misses its pharma context, without What nobody can tell whether it worked, and without How it is soon forgotten.

Next: Two examples, one order ↓

Part 3 of 4 · Concrete Practice · about 2 min

Two examples, one order

Here are two very different pieces of work: a real bachelor course at SDU, and an imagined People Development workshop for the teachers of a real master's course at UCPH. Both follow the same order (anchor, assess and target, deliver) and each part of that order uses one model.

Both courses are real. The workshop, the starting levels, the targets and the session designs are illustrative, written to show the method.

Curriculum coursePeople Development

  1. 1

    Anchor

    Uses Pharma Value Chain

    Place it in the value chain. This sets what is in scope.

    Curriculum course · FA516 course

    Molecular property prediction, used to rank compounds before a candidate is chosen: Lead Optimisation & Candidate Selection (Pre-clinical)

    People Development · SMPS20003U teachers' workshop

    Trial-protocol teaching, where designs are powered, analysed and reported: Phase I / II / III (Clinical development)
  2. 2

    Assess and target

    Uses PDS Competence Model

    Estimate today's level for two or three competencies and choose targets.

    Curriculum course · FA516 course

    • Model assessment and sensitivity analysis L1 to →L3
    • Reproducible Analysis L2 to →L3

    People Development · SMPS20003U teachers' workshop

    • Hypothesis testing L2 to →L3
    • What can AI be used for? What can it not be used for? L1 to →L2
  3. 3

    Deliver

    Uses Pedagogic Practices

    Plan each session as a 4Cs sequence and check its blocks against the Six Trumps.

    Curriculum course · FA516 course

    Each two-hour exercise session is planned as a 4Cs sequence. Its practice block feeds the group project. Connections → Concepts → Concrete Practice → Conclusions

    People Development · SMPS20003U teachers' workshop

    Two half-day workshops. Teachers practise on the medical case they set their own students. Connections → Concepts → Concrete Practice → Concrete Practice → Conclusions

Try it

Take the course or workshop you thought of at the start. Which substep of the value chain does it point to? Pick two or three competencies and estimate today's level and a target. Then sketch one session as a 4Cs sequence: one block for each C.

Next: The map ↓

Part 4 of 4 · Conclusions · about 3 min

The map

Put the first two models side by side and you get a grid: the 14 value-chain substeps run across and the 7 competence domains run down.

The grid has no fixed links. CPDSE does not keep a list of competencies for each substep. A mark appears only where a course or workshop sets a target, and the four marks here come from the two illustrative examples. The 4Cs are how the teaching is planned to reach each target.

What a CPDSE-teacher does next

  • Anchor your next course or workshop: find its substep in the value chain.
  • Assess and target: choose two or three competencies in the competence model and read what each level means.
  • Deliver: plan each session as a 4Cs sequence and check its blocks against the Six Trumps.
